items.title: Q1 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit I: Drama · Luigi Pirandello
items.stem:
When uigi Pirandello’s Six Characters in Search of an Author opens the audience find the
producer attempting to stage a play. What is the title of this play ?
items.explanation: In the metatheatrical opening of Luigi Pirandello's Six Characters in Search of an Author (1921), the acting company and the Director are interrupted while rehearsing Pirandello's own earlier comedy, The Rules of the Game (Il giuoco delle parti, 1918).

items.title: Q2 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Which Canterbury pilgrim carries a brooch inscribed ith the atin ords eaning “Love
Conquers All” ?
items.explanation: In the General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales, Geoffrey Chaucer describes the elegant Prioress (Madame Eglentyne) as wearing a golden brooch upon which was engraved a crowned 'A' with the Latin motto 'Amor vincit omnia' ('Love conquers all').

items.title: Q3 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin, Thomas Hardy
items.stem:
In his Introduction to The Oxford Book of Twentieth-Century English Verse (1973), Philip arkin
underlines the importance of a native tradition ith __________ seen as the ajor poet of
the Modern Period.
items.explanation: In his influential Introduction to The Oxford Book of Twentieth-Century English Verse (1973), Philip Larkin championed the insular native British poetic tradition over cosmopolitan modernism, establishing Thomas Hardy as the central, indispensable master of modern English poetry.

items.title: Q4 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
Philip Sidney defended poetry against such descriptions of it as “the other of lies” and “the
nurse of abuse.” His ain argument here is __________ .
options: The poet is no conjuror or illusionist and represents a orld.
The poet cannot lie because he is not claiming to tell us the truth.
The poet cannot speak the truth because he is not representing the real orld.
The poet is a philosopher for hom truth is a lie, and lie truth, in an imaginary orld.
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry (1595), Sir Philip Sidney rebuts Stephen Gosson's charge that poets are the 'fathers of lies' by asserting that 'the poet he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth', since he presents imaginative fictions rather than asserting literal factual truths.

items.title: Q5 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Chapter III of Oliver Twist opens ith a narratorial remark about Oliver being punished for
“the commission of the impious and profane offence of asking for ore.” What did Oliver
ask for ore ?
items.explanation: In Chapter II-III of Charles Dickens's Oliver Twist (1838), the famished workhouse boys cast lots and Oliver famously approaches the master with his basin and spoon, uttering 'Please, sir, I want some more' gruel to eat, which the workhouse board treats as an impious outrage.

items.title: Q6 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser
items.stem:
Edmund Spenser’s Epithalamion is a carefully structured poem carrying L__________
corresponding to the __________ .
options: twelve stanzas; onths of the year
three hundred and sixty five lines; days of the year
fourteen stanzas; two eek-long bridal ceremonies
items.explanation: Edmund Spenser's Epithalamion (1595) is meticulously structured around the calendar and diurnal cycles: its 24 stanzas represent the 24 hours of midsummer day, and its 365 long lines correspond mathematically to the days of the year.

items.title: Q7 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Choose the right chronological sequence below :
options: Victorian Period – Jacobean Period – Tudor Period – Restoration Period
Edwardian Period – Tudor Period – Jacobean Period – Victorian Period
Tudor Period – Jacobean Period – Restoration Period – Edwardian Period
Jacobean Period – Tudor Period – Restoration Period – Edwardian Period
items.explanation: The proper chronological succession of English literary periods is Tudor Period (1485–1603) followed by Jacobean Period (1603–1625), Restoration Period (1660–1700), and Edwardian Period (1901–1910).

items.title: Q8 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem:
“That oman’s days ere spent
In ignorant ood – ill,
Her nights in argument
Until her voice rew shrill” (W. B. Yeats : “Easter 1916”)
Who is the poet referring to ?
items.explanation: In 'Easter, 1916', W. B. Yeats devotes his second stanza to Countess Constance Markievicz (née Gore-Booth), lamenting how her youthful beauty was consumed by political shrillness: 'That woman’s days were spent / In ignorant good-will, / Her nights in argument / Until her voice grew shrill.'

items.title: Q9 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following as replaced by Communicative anguage Teaching ?
items.explanation: Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) arose in the late 1960s and 1970s primarily in reaction against British Situational Language Teaching and the Audiolingual/Structural Approach; both Options 2 and 4 represent historical predecessors superseded by CLT, prompting UGC to award marks to all.

items.title: Q10 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
To hom does Francis Bacon offer the following piece of advice ?
“Let him sequester himself from the Company of his Countrymen, and diet in such Places,
here there is good company of the Nation... Let him upon his Removes, ... procure
Recommendation, to some person of Quality, residing in the Place, hither he removeth...”
items.explanation: In his essay 'Of Travel' (1625), Francis Bacon advises the young gentleman traveller to avoid cloistering with fellow countrymen, to eat where there is local company, and to carry letters of recommendation to persons of quality at every stop.

items.title: Q11 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Richard Hooker
items.stem:
In his asterpiece, Of the awes of Ecclesiasticall Politie, Richard Hooker affirmed the Anglican
tradition as that of a “threefold cord not quickly broken.” He specifically referred to the
following EXCEPT __________ .
items.explanation: In Of the Lawes of Ecclesiasticall Politie (1594), Anglican theologian Richard Hooker formulated the classic Anglican theological tripod or 'threefold cord' consisting of Scripture, Reason, and Tradition; 'community' was not one of the three components.

items.title: Q12 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit II: Poetry · Christina Rossetti, Matthew Arnold, Robert Browning, Arthur Hugh Clough
items.stem:

ist – I
ist – II

items.explanation: Christina Rossetti's Goblin Market relates Laura's temptation and Lizzie's moral resistance (iii); Arnold's Sohrab and Rustum narrates a father unknowingly slaying his son (i); Browning's The Ring and the Book presents a 17th-century murder via multiple monologues (iv); and Clough's The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich describes an Oxford reading party in Scotland (ii).

items.title: Q13 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Blake
items.stem:
“Beneath them sit the aged en, ise uardians of the poor;
Then cherish pity, lest you drive an angel from your door.”
These concluding lines of William Blake’s Innocence poem called “Holy
Thursday” allude to a Biblical passage. Identify the passage.
options: The angel of the ord encampeth round about those ho fear Him and delivereth them. Psalms 34.7
Suffer not thy outh to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it as an error. Ecclesiastes 5.6
And they said unto her, Thou art ad. But she constantly affirmed that it as even so. Then said they, It is his angel. The Acts 12.15
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. Hebrews 13.2
items.explanation: The closing moral of William Blake's 'Holy Thursday' in Songs of Innocence ('Then cherish pity, lest you drive an angel from your door') directly echoes Hebrews 13:2: 'Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.'

items.title: Q14 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Direct Method of anguage Teaching involves :
(a)
the use of Target anguage only
(b)
repetition of exercises
(c)
linguistic correctness
(d)
problem solving exercises
In relation to the above hich of the following is correct ?
items.explanation: The Direct Method of language teaching relies on immersion in the target language without mother-tongue translation (a), continuous oral practice and repetition (b), and accurate sentence patterns (c).

items.title: Q15 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit II: Poetry · Derek Walcott
items.stem:
In hich of the following orks does the narrator proclaim, “either I’ nobody, or I’ the
nation” ?
options: George amming’s In the Castle of My Skin
items.explanation: In Derek Walcott's acclaimed autobiographical poem 'The Schooner Flight' (1979), the mulatto sailor Shabine declares: 'I'm just a red nigger who love the sea, / I had a sound colonial education, / I have Dutch, nigger, and English in me, / and either I'm nobody, or I'm a nation.'

items.title: Q16 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Like Cordelia, the Fool in King ear is __________ .
options: referred to by ear as his child.
punished for not telling the truth.
items.explanation: Throughout Shakespeare's King Lear, Lear tenderly refers to his Fool as 'boy', 'pretty knave', and 'my child', culminating in his agonizing final-scene conflation of grief: 'And my poor fool is hang'd! No, no, no life!'

items.title: Q17 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Arun Joshi
items.stem:
Sindi Oberoi, the narrator hero in Arun Joshi’s The Foreigner says : “My foreignness lay ithin
e and I couldn’t leave yself behind herever I ent.” Identify the countries hich Sindi
Oberoi ent to.
options: Kenya, Uganda, New Zealand, England, India
items.explanation: In Arun Joshi's existential novel The Foreigner (1968), the rootless protagonist Sindi (Surinder) Oberoi is born in Kenya, moves to Uganda, studies in England, works in Boston (America), and finally migrates to India in search of detachment and selfhood.

items.title: Q18 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Toni Morrison
items.stem:
Assertion (A) :
The orld does not become raceless or ill not become unracialized by
assertion. The act of enforcing racelessness in literary discourse is itself a
racial act.
Reason (R) :
Pouring rhetorical acid on the fingers of a black hand ay indeed destroy
the prints, but not the hand. Besides, hat happens, in that violent, self-
serving act of erasure, to the hands, the fingers, the fingerprints of the one
ho does the pouring ? Do they remain acid-free ? The literature itself
suggests otherwise.
In the context of the statements above,
options: (A) akes complete sense in the light of (R).
items.explanation: In Playing in the Dark: Whiteness and the Literary Imagination (1992), Toni Morrison argues that enforcing racelessness in American literary study is itself an aggressive act of racial erasure; Assertion (A) is fully substantiated by Reason (R)'s caustic metaphor of pouring rhetorical acid.

items.title: Q19 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit II: Poetry · Alfred Lord Tennyson
items.stem:
A poet laureate said “I do not think that since Shakespeare there has been such a aster of
the English language as I.” Who is the poet ?
items.explanation: Alfred Lord Tennyson, Victorian Poet Laureate from 1850 until his death in 1892, famously boasted of his supreme auditory and verbal craft: 'I do not think that since Shakespeare there has been such a master of the English language as I.'

items.title: Q20 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Jeremy Taylor, John Milton
items.stem:
Who among the following was a contemporary of John Milton and wrote The Worthy
Communicant ? It is said that his prose “can be read easily, hen Milton’s ust be studied.”
items.explanation: Jeremy Taylor (1613–1667), author of The Worthy Communicant (1660) as well as Holy Living and Holy Dying, was renowned for his lucid, musical prose style, often contrasted with the Latinate syntactical complexity of his contemporary John Milton.

items.title: Q21 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dryden
items.stem:
In L1668, Dryden wrote Of Dramatic Poesie : An Essay which uses__________ separate
characters to dramatise the conflicting viewpoints hich new theatrical activity had produced.
items.explanation: John Dryden's Of Dramatic Poesy: An Essay (1668) stages a polite debate among four gentlemanly speakers on a barge on the Thames: Crites (advocating Ancients), Eugenius (Moderns), Lisideius (French drama), and Neander (representing Dryden, defending modern English drama).

items.title: Q22 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit I: Drama · August Strindberg
items.stem:
Writing his ost influential play, August Strindberg called it “My ost beloved drama, the
child of y reatest suffering.” The play is :
items.explanation: Swedish dramatist August Strindberg designated A Dream Play (Ett drömspel, 1901) as 'my most beloved drama, the child of my greatest suffering', pioneering an expressionistic, dreamlike dramaturgy where time and space dissolve.

items.title: Q23 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Virginia Woolf
items.stem:
In hich essay does Virginia Woolf observe that “if a riter ere a free an [sic] and not a
slave” to the conventions of the literary arket-place, there ould be “no plot, no comedy,
no tragedy, no love interest, or catastrophe in the accepted style, and perhaps not a single
button sewn on as the Bond Street tailors ould have it” ?
items.explanation: In her landmark essay 'Modern Fiction' (1919/1925), Virginia Woolf critiques Edwardian materialists (Bennett, Galsworthy, Wells) and asserts that if a writer were free, there would be 'no plot, no comedy, no tragedy... and perhaps not a single button sewn on as the Bond Street tailors would have it.'

items.title: Q24 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Keats
items.stem:
In his famous letter to Benjamin Bailey (November 22, 1817) John Keats rote : “I am certain
of nothing but the holiness of the Heart’s affections and the truth of Imagination - What the
imagination seizes as Beauty ust be truth.” Which of the following sentences follows this
passage ?
options: Now I am sensible all this is a ere sophistication, however it ay neighbour to any truths, to excuse y own indolence...
The Imagination ay be compared to Adam’s dream - he oke and found it true.
This however I am persuaded of, that nothing beside Imagination can ive us sweet sensations and pleasurable thoughts.
My pains at last some respite shall afford, hile I behold the battles Imagination aintains.
items.explanation: In his letter to Benjamin Bailey on 22 November 1817, after writing that 'What the imagination seizes as Beauty must be truth', Keats immediately adds the famous analogy: 'The Imagination may be compared to Adam’s dream - he woke and found it truth' (alluding to Paradise Lost Book VIII).

items.title: Q25 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Which of the following pair best describes the characteristic features of Marlowe’s portrait of
Tamburlaine ?
(a)
ambition
(b)
apathy
(c)
cruelty
(d)
sympathy
The right combination according to the code is __________ .
items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great (Parts 1 & 2, 1587) characterizes the Scythian shepherd-conqueror through soaring, overreaching ambition (a) and ruthless, merciless cruelty (c) toward his defeated captives.

items.title: Q26 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Oscar Wilde
items.stem:
Who is the author of the statement : “The nineteenth century dislike of Realism is the rage of
Caliban seeing his own face in the lass” ?
items.explanation: In the famous aphoristic Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), Oscar Wilde writes: 'The nineteenth century dislike of Realism is the rage of Caliban seeing his own face in a glass. The nineteenth century dislike of Romanticism is the rage of Caliban not seeing his own face in a glass.'

items.title: Q27 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Thomas Mann
items.stem:
Which of the following statements about Thomas Mann’s novels is true ?
(a)
Buddenbrooks is a family saga set in the early decades of the twentieth century.
(b)
Aschenbach, the riter protagonist in Death in Venice, is preoccupied ith classicism,
especially ith classical ideals of ale beauty.
(c)
In his second inter at the sanatorium, Hans Castorp, protagonist of The Magic Mountain
ets lost in a blizzard during a solitary skiing expedition.
(d)
Adrian everkuhn, the odern day Faustus in Mann’s Doctor Faustus is a usician.
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: In Thomas Mann's works, Death in Venice features Aschenbach's obsession with classical aesthetic ideals (b); The Magic Mountain features Castorp's visionary blizzard ski journey in 'Snow' (c); and Doctor Faustus features modern composer Adrian Leverkühn (d). Statement (a) is incorrect because Buddenbrooks is set across the 19th century (1835–1877).

items.title: Q28 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit VI: English in India · Raja Ram Mohan Roy
items.stem:
To hom did Raja Ram Mohan Roy rite in 1823 his letter seeking the introduction of
English education in India ?
items.explanation: In December 1823, Indian social reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy addressed his historic letter advocating modern European scientific and English education (rather than government funds being wasted on traditional Sanskrit paths) to Governor-General Lord Amherst.

items.title: Q29 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit III: Fiction, short story · John Bunyan
items.stem:
Listed below are the seemingly friendly characters in The Pilgrim’s Progress ho ive Christian
dangerous advice. Among them is one ho does not belong to this roup. Identify this odd
character.
items.explanation: In John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), Evangelist is Christian's trusted spiritual mentor who sets him on the narrow path to the Wicket Gate, whereas Mr. Worldly Wiseman, Ignorance, and Talkative provide perilous and false advice.

items.title: Q30 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Classical & Ancient Background · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Aristotle
items.stem:
Aristotle argued that poetry provides a/an __________ outlet for the release of intense
emotions.
items.explanation: In the Poetics, Aristotle argues that tragic drama provides a safe and cathartic outlet (katharsis) for the purging and healthy regulation of intense pity and fear, directly countering Plato's claim that poetry excites irrational passions dangerously.

items.title: Q31 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
The direct French influence on the English language during the Middle English period as
in the form of __________ .
options: intake of French ords into English.
both the loss of inflections and intake of French ords into English.
items.explanation: The direct lexical consequence of the Norman Conquest during Middle English was the massive intake of Anglo-Norman and French vocabulary into English, whereas the loss of inflectional endings was an internal Germanic phonological development accelerated by earlier Old Norse contact.

items.title: Q32 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
A significant development in 1662 as the establishment of The Royal Society in England.
The ain purpose of the society as __________ .
options: to set the rules for the royal court and overnance
to uide and promote the development of science and scientific exploration
to set norms for civil society
items.explanation: Founded in 1660 and granted its royal charter by King Charles II in 1662, The Royal Society of London was established for 'Improving Natural Knowledge', guiding experimental science and empirical inquiry through its famous motto 'Nullius in verba'.

items.title: Q33 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · William Cowper
items.stem:
William Cowper rote in The Task (IV. 681-82) about those ho “Build factories ith blood,
conducting trade/At the sword’s point ...” These lines allude to :
options: West Indian slave-plantation owners and the East India Company ‘nabobs’
Exploiters of child labour in the ondon suburbs
items.explanation: In Book IV of The Task (1785), William Cowper condemns imperial greed and colonial exploitation, specifically excoriating the sugar plantation slaveholders of the West Indies and the corrupt, predatory 'nabobs' of the British East India Company.

items.title: Q34 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
The commedia dell’arte originated in Italy in the sixteenth century. Which of the following
descriptions are the ost appropriate ?
(a)
Tears alternating ith crude laughter
(b)
Comedy of the uild or by the professionals in the “art”
(c)
Plautine comedy alternating ith ritualistic anoeuvres
(d)
Improvised comedy that follows a scenario rather than ritten dialogue
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: Originating in 16th-century Italy, commedia dell'arte literally means comedy of the professional craft or guild (b), featuring masked stock types performing improvised action based on an outlined scenario or canovaccio (d).

items.title: Q35 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
“Nature and Nature’s aws lay hid in Night,
God said et Newton be! And all as ight.”
Alexander Pope’s famous couplet impressively captures __________.
options: Newton’s confirmation of the Genesis passage here God ordains ight
Newton’s empirical observations of Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica
Newton’s application of principles of otion to account for any natural phenomena
Newton’s discovery that all colours are contained in hite light
items.explanation: Alexander Pope's epitaph intended for Sir Isaac Newton ('Nature and Nature's Laws lay hid in Night; / God said, Let Newton be! and all was Light') brilliantly celebrates both Newton's optics (demonstrating that white light contains the entire visible spectrum) and his universal laws of gravitation.

items.title: Q36 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Eugene O'Neill, Susan Glaspell
items.stem:
What as the name of the experimental theatre roup founded in 1915 by Susan Glaspell,
Eugene O’Neill and other dramatists in order to challenge Broadway’s control over American
drama ?
items.explanation: The Provincetown Players was an avant-garde theatrical collective founded in 1915 on Cape Cod by Susan Glaspell, George Cram Cook, and Eugene O'Neill, pioneering modern American serious drama away from the commercial formulas of Broadway.

items.title: Q37 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Jonathan Swift
items.stem:
After his return from the land of Houyhnhnms, Gulliver refused to let his ife and children
__________ .
options: touch his bread, or drink out of his cup.
communicate ith him in English tongue.
items.explanation: In Part IV Chapter XI of Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), Lemuel Gulliver returns from the Houyhnhnms with such profound misanthropic disgust toward human Yahoos that for years he forbids his wife and children to touch his bread or drink from his cup.

items.title: Q38 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas De Quincey, William Wordsworth
items.stem:
In hich of the following volumes do you find a charming appreciation of the Wordsworth
household by Thomas de Quincey ?
options: The Confessions of an English Opium-Eater
Lives and etters, Far Away and ong Ago
Notes on My ake Country Evenings
Reminiscences of the English ake Poets
items.explanation: Thomas De Quincey published his intimate and vivid memoirs of William and Dorothy Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and Robert Southey in a celebrated series of essays in Tait's Edinburgh Magazine, later collected as Reminiscences of the English Lake Poets.

items.title: Q39 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Frank Kermode
items.stem:
One of the ost highly revered, scholarly, and passionate interpreters of English and orld
literatures, he as appointed the ord Northcliffe Professor of Modern English iterature at

Not Entitled in 1995. The epigraph to this book came from Coriolanus : “He as a kind of
nothing, titleless.”
Who among the following is this riter/critic ?
items.explanation: Distinguished scholar Sir Frank Kermode held both the Lord Northcliffe Chair at UCL and the King Edward VII Chair at Cambridge, was knighted in 1991, and published his reflective memoir Not Entitled in 1995 using Coriolanus's line 'He was a kind of nothing, titleless' as epigraph.

items.title: Q40 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Which of the following provided theoretical basis for Audio-Lingual Method of anguage
Teaching ?
options: Behaviourist Psychology and Bloomfieldian Structural inguistics
items.explanation: The Audio-Lingual Method (ALM) of second language teaching emerged during World War II, resting theoretically on B. F. Skinner's stimulus-response Behaviourist psychology and Leonard Bloomfield's structural, descriptive linguistics.

items.title: Q41 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit I: Drama · Anton Chekhov
items.stem:
Who among the following characters of The Cherry Orchard by Anton Chekhov dies in the
final scene ?
items.explanation: At the conclusion of Anton Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard (1904), the household departs and locks up the estate, inadvertently stranding the aged, ailing manservant Firs inside, who lies down quietly and expires as the sound of an axe chopping cherry trees echoes.

items.title: Q42 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Thomas Gray, John Milton
items.stem:
In tracing the history of English poetry, Thomas Gray’s “Progress of Poesy” invokes a ajor
poet as follows :
“Nor second He, that rode sublime
Upon the seraph-wings of Extasy,
The secrets of th’ Abyss to spy.”
Who is “He” ?
items.explanation: In Thomas Gray's Pindaric ode 'The Progress of Poesy' (1757), Shakespeare is depicted first as Nature's darling, followed by John Milton ('Nor second He, that rode sublime / Upon the seraph-wings of Extasy, / The secrets of th' Abyss to spy'), celebrating Paradise Lost.

items.title: Q43 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Samuel Johnson
items.stem:
“I suffered from impaired eye-sight, depression and poverty and left Oxford ithout a degree.
After a period as a teacher and y arriage to a idow twice y age, I left for ondon, to

items.title: Q44 · June 2015 (Paper III)

items.title: Q45 · June 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dryden
items.stem:
In John Dryden’s Essay on Dramatic Poesy Neander defends the English invention
of L__________.
items.explanation: In John Dryden's Of Dramatic Poesy: An Essay (1668), Neander (Dryden's surrogate) famously champions English theatrical variety against rigid French Neoclassicism, passionately defending the English invention and mastery of tragicomedy as combining mirth with serious pathos.

items.explanation: H. M. Green published the monumental two-volume study A History of Australian Literature: Pure and Applied in 1961, which remains the foundational critical and bibliographic survey of Australian literary history from 1789 to 1950.

items.title: Q54 · June 2015 (Paper III)

The Voice

Saying that now you are not as what you were
When you had changed from the one who was all to me
But as first, when our day was fair

Can it be you that I hear ? Let me view you, then
Standing as when I drew near to the town
Where you would wait for me : yes, as I knew you then,
Even to the original air-blue gown!

Or is it only the breeze, in its listlessness
Travelling across the wet mead to me here,
You being ever dissolved to wan wistlessness
Heard no more again far or near ?

Thus I; faltering forward,
Leaves around me falling,
Wind oozing thin through the thorn from norward
And the woman calling.

items.explanation: In the opening stanza of 'The Voice' ('Woman much missed, how you call to me... Saying that now you are not as what you were / When you had changed... But as first, when our day was fair'), Hardy establishes a stark temporal contrast between the desolate present ('now') and their bright past ('then').
